content.body: Have you ever wondered how a messaging app knows if '12' could be 'AB' (1,2) or 'L' (12)? Let's learn to decode number strings like '226' into letters. We'll discover a clever way to remember what we've already calculated.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply a memoization technique to avoid redundant calculations.
• Implement a function that counts ways to decode a numeric string.
• Explain why storing results in a lookup structure improves efficiency.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: For the string '12', how many ways can we decode it? (A=1, B=2, ..., L=12)
content.successMessage: Nice! '12' can be 'AB' (1,2) or 'L' (12), so 2 ways.

content.title: Try a longer string
content.prompt: For '226', how many ways? Check all possible splits like 2|26, 22|6, etc.
content.successMessage: Well done! Possible decodings: BBF (2,2,6), BZ (2,26), VF (22,6). That's 3 ways.

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Great! You likely checked many combinations: AAAA (1,1,1,1), KAA (11,1,1), AKA (1,11,1), etc. That's 5 total.

content.body: What you just did was explore all possible splits by checking each position and trying one or two digits. For longer strings, this becomes very slow because you re-check the same substrings many times.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Imagine a string like '1111111111' (ten 1's). The number of possibilities grows exponentially, and recalculating for each substring repeatedly is inefficient. We need a better method. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of recalculating, we can store results for substrings we've already solved in a lookup structure (like an object or Map). This way, we check our notebook before doing new work.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use recursion with memoization. For each position in the string, we try decoding one digit (if valid) and two digits (if valid), store the result for that position, and reuse it.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample: Walkthrough with '226': Start at index 0 → try '2' (valid) → solve substring from index 1. Try '22' (valid) → solve substring from index 2. Store results: memo[0] = memo[1] + memo[2]. Reuse stored results when revisiting indexes.

content.body:
1. Create a memo object to store results for each index.
2. Define a recursive helper function that takes an index.
3. If index is at the end, return 1 (one way found).
4. If result for this index is in memo, return it.
5. Try one-digit decode (if valid), add ways from next index.
6. Try two-digit decode (if valid), add ways from index+2.
7. Store total ways in memo for this index and return it.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create function and memo
steps.instruction: Start by declaring the main function numDecodings that takes a string s. Inside, create an empty object called memo to store results for indexes.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function declaration and memo object created.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the storage for our results.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure you declare both the function and the memo object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function and a place to remember results.

steps.title: Define recursive helper
steps.instruction: Inside numDecodings, define a helper function called dfs that takes an index i. It will return the number of ways to decode from position i to the end.
steps.expectedOutcome: Helper function dfs declared inside numDecodings.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we have our recursive explorer.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the function definition syntax. It should take one parameter i.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember, we need a function inside numDecodings that we can call recursively.

steps.title: Add base case and memo check
steps.instruction: Inside dfs, first handle the base case: if i equals s.length, return 1 (one valid decoding found). Then, check if memo[i] exists; if so, return memo[i] immediately.
steps.hint: Use if (i === s.length) return 1; and if (memo[i] !== undefined) return memo[i];
steps.expectedOutcome: Base case and memo lookup implemented in dfs.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! This prevents recalculating work we've already done.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you check both conditions in the correct order.
steps.feedbackWrong: Think about when we reach the end and when we can use stored results.

steps.title: Try one-digit and two-digit decodes
steps.instruction: Still inside dfs, initialize a variable ways to 0. Check if the one-digit substring s[i] is not '0' (valid). If valid, add dfs(i+1) to ways. Then check if the two-digit substring s[i] + s[i+1] exists and is between '10' and '26'. If valid, add dfs(i+2) to ways.
steps.hint: Use let ways = 0; then if (s[i] !== '0') ways += dfs(i+1); then if (i+1 < s.length && ...) ways += dfs(i+2);
steps.expectedOutcome: Logic to try valid one-digit and two-digit decodes added.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! You're exploring both possibilities at each step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the conditions for valid one-digit and two-digit numbers.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember, '0' is invalid alone, and two-digit numbers must be 10-26.

steps.title: Store result and return
steps.instruction: After calculating ways, store it in memo[i], then return ways. Finally, at the end of numDecodings, return dfs(0) to start the recursion from the beginning.
steps.hint: Add memo[i] = ways; return ways; and return dfs(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: Memo storage and final return added; function is complete.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Congratulations! You've built a memoized decoder.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to store the result in memo and start the recursion.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to save the result for this index and initiate the process.

content.body: You've successfully implemented the Decode Ways algorithm using memoization! Remember: the key was storing results in a lookup structure (memo) to avoid redundant work. This pattern of 'remember what we've already seen' is powerful for many problems where subproblems repeat.
